hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
hero.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreemen
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

 The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

 Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

 Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said.

 "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.

cards.headline: More Than 100 Cats Rescued From Port St. Lucie Hoarding House
cards.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens are now receiving medical care and nourishment after being pulled from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the Humane Society of St. Lucie shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie, said many of the cats arrived in poor health. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. Wees said staff are still sorting out which cats belong to which litters. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was called in quickly after Wees reached out. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the extra support is already paying off, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," she said.

St. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed. The Humane Society of St. Lucie is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they continue treatment and work toward foster placement and adoption.

cards.headline: Rescued Hobe Sound Kittens Buried Alive Recovering in Foster Care
cards.teaser: Kali and Amara, the two kittens pulled alive from a backyard burial site in Hobe Sound, are gaining strength with a foster family and could be ready for adoption within weeks.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek on Friday gave new details on the arrest of a Hobe Sound woman accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive, revealing that deputies heard the animals crying from beneath the ground during a backyard search. Alba Chavez, 36, faces four felony counts of animal torture after deputies said she buried kittens up to 3 feet underground at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park, with two kittens rescued alive and two found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property.

Deputies responded to the mobile home park Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, fearing for three remaining kittens, had locked them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. When they returned, they found the bedroom door forced open and the kittens gone, prompting the call to law enforcement. Deputies found Chavez standing in the roadway, and she reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens, telling deputies she believed the animals had demons, calling them ugly and saying she did not want black or brown cats in the home.

Chavez then led deputies to the backyard where the kittens had been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As deputies dug through the rain-soaked ground, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were pulled out alive and rushed to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries from lack of oxygen while the animals were buried, and he said the kittens could still die from their injuries despite being rescued. The two kittens killed Monday were found dead at the burial site.

Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, corresponding to the two kittens found dead and the two found alive. She is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also has an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined how the first two kittens died or established a motive for Chavez's actions. Budensiek said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. The sheriff said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the missing fifth kitten is found dead. The Florida Department of Children and Families became involved following the incident, and the children were released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

cards.headline: Three generations later, Packard Roofing remains rooted on the Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: Founded in Miami in 1971 and established on the Treasure Coast in 1994, Packard Roofing & Waterproofing is now led by third-generation siblings Brian Packard and Stephanie Packard Smith.
cards.body:
For the Packard family, roofing has never been simply a business passed from one generation to the next. It has been a trade learned firsthand, a family responsibility and, over time, a connection to the communities the company serves.

 Packard Roofing & Waterproofing has grown from a South Florida roofing company into a multigenerational operation serving homeowners across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 The Port St. Lucie family business was founded in Miami in 1971 by Raymond M. Packard and David R. Packard. More than two decades later, the company expanded to Port St. Lucie in 1994, establishing the Treasure Coast operation that now serves customers across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

 Today, the company is led by third-generation siblings Brian Packard and Stephanie Packard Smith.

 Brian's path into the family business started well before he was old enough to run one. As a teenager, he spent summers cleaning and organizing the warehouse and service yard. Later came tear-off crews, repair work, and eventually handling residential and commercial projects himself.

 Stephanie's history with the company also stretches back decades. She joined during the hectic aftermath of Hurricane Andrew in 1992, when South Florida roofing companies were dealing with enormous demand while Packard Roofing was also recovering from storm damage to its own facilities. She went on to become a central part of the company's office operations.

 Brian relocated from Miami to Port St. Lucie in 2021 as the family prepared for another transition. Following their father David Packard's death in 2022, Brian and Stephanie took responsibility for leading the company into its third generation.

 A business built around the Treasure Coast

 Packard Roofing's headquarters at 2182 NW Reserve Park Trace places the company beside PGA Village in Port St. Lucie, with much of its work concentrated throughout the Treasure Coast.

 The company handles roof repairs, roof replacements, new roof construction, and maintenance for homeowners throughout Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

 That local focus matters in a region where roofs face intense sun, heavy rainfall, tropical weather, and wind-driven rain. For homeowners, problems can range from persistent leaks and storm damage to aging roofs that have reached the end of their useful lifespan.

 Packard Roofing's website also provides homeowners with information about issues such as hurricane preparation, wind damage, roof leaks, and deciding when a roof should be repaired rather than replaced.

 For a company with decades behind it, that focus reflects an effort to remain useful to homeowners before they ever need a major roofing project.

 Experience that stayed with the company

 The Packard family is not the only long-term presence in the business.

 Superintendent Mark Hanna has worked with the company for more than 30 years, beginning as a repairman before moving into a leadership role overseeing repair and replacement work. His responsibilities now include supervising projects, preparing estimates, and often serving as one of the first people customers meet when they contact the company.

 That kind of employee longevity fits the broader story of a company that has transitioned across three generations without abandoning its family-business identity.

 Packard's philosophy, according to the family, has remained centered on straightforward communication, quality materials, and workmanship the company is willing to stand behind. The company says many customers return when they move to another home or recommend Packard to younger generations of their own families.

 Looking toward another generation

 More than five decades after the company was founded, Packard Roofing is operating in a Treasure Coast that looks very different from the one it entered in the 1990s.

 Port St. Lucie has grown around it. PGA Village and surrounding communities have expanded. New homes continue to rise while existing roofs move through the repair and replacement cycle that comes with age and Florida weather.

 The business has changed with that growth, but its leadership still describes Packard in distinctly family terms.

 For Brian, continuing the company means carrying forward standards established by his grandfather and father rather than simply preserving a business name. He has described honesty, hard work and quality craftsmanship as values passed down through three generations.

 Packard Roofing & Waterproofing provides roof repair, replacement, maintenance, and new-roof construction throughout Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

hero.headline: More Than 100 Cats Rescued From Port St. Lucie Hoarding House
hero.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens are now receiving medical care and nourishment after being pulled from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the Humane Society of St. Lucie shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie, said many of the cats arrived in poor health. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. Wees said staff are still sorting out which cats belong to which litters. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was called in quickly after Wees reached out. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the extra support is already paying off, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," she said.

St. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed. The Humane Society of St. Lucie is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they continue treatment and work toward foster placement and adoption.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
hero.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreemen
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

 The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

 Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

 Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said.

 "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.
